The San, historically called Bushmen. The indigenous hunter-gatherer peoples of southern Africa with one of the oldest continuous cultures, renowned for exceptional tracking knowledge, distinctive language features, and rock art spanning tens of thousands of years. The San inhabited southern Africa, in what is now South Africa, Botswana, Namibia, and surrounding regions, for at least twenty thousand years before Bantu migrations and European colonization. They speak Khoisan languages featuring distinctive click consonants—four to five different click types produced by the tongue, teeth, or palate. These sounds distinguish their languages from all surrounding African language families. The San practiced specialized hunting and gathering with unmatched tracking skills, accumulating deep ecological knowledge of game animals, water sources, and edible plants across diverse landscapes. They created extraordinary rock art including rock paintings and engravings spanning over forty thousand years, depicting animals, human figures, and spiritual visions. Many of these sites remain sacred to the San today. They developed trance dance rituals for healing, spiritual communication, and community bonding, with shamanic practitioners holding high status in their societies. However, the San faced severe marginalization and violence under colonial rule and post-colonial governments. Many were displaced from ancestral lands and confined to marginal territories. Today, the San population numbers roughly one hundred thousand to one hundred fifty thousand across southern Africa. Language and cultural preservation efforts remain ongoing as they work to maintain their heritage.
